concept.body: The four-center table. Circumcenter: perpendicular bisectors, equidistant from VERTICES, circle around. Incenter: angle bisectors, equidistant from SIDES, circle inside. Centroid: medians, BALANCE point. Orthocenter: altitudes. Match by the LINES or by the PROPERTY, whichever the problem gives.

explanationVariants: Equidistant from the VERTICES is the circumcenter (perpendicular bisectors).

widget.prompt: Which center is equidistant from all three VERTICES?

options.label: circumcenter
options.feedback: Perpendicular bisectors make it equidistant from the vertices — the circumscribed-circle center.

options.label: incenter
options.feedback: The incenter is equidistant from the SIDES, not vertices. Vertices → circumcenter.

options.label: centroid
options.feedback: The centroid is the balance point, not equidistant from vertices. That's the circumcenter.

options.label: orthocenter
options.feedback: The orthocenter has no equidistance property. Equidistant from vertices is the circumcenter.

steps.body: Four centers, four jobs. **Circumcenter** (perpendicular bisectors) — equidistant from vertices. **Incenter** (angle bisectors) — equidistant from sides. **Centroid** (medians) — balance point. **Orthocenter** (altitudes) — altitudes' meeting. Knowing the defining LINES and PROPERTY of each is the whole chapter.

widget.prompt: Sort each center by the lines that define it.

items.label: circumcenter (perpendicular bisectors)
items.feedback: Perpendicular bisectors are a bisector family — they cut sides in half at right angles.

items.label: incenter (angle bisectors)
items.feedback: Angle bisectors split angles — a bisector family.

items.label: centroid (medians)
items.feedback: Medians run from each VERTEX to the opposite midpoint — vertex-based.

items.label: orthocenter (altitudes)
items.feedback: Altitudes drop from each VERTEX perpendicular to the opposite side — vertex-based.

widget.missFeedback: Bisectors (perpendicular-bisector, angle-bisector) vs vertex-based lines (medians, altitudes).
widget.successFeedback: Two bisector centers, two vertex-line centers.

explanationVariants: Equidistant from the three SIDES is the incenter (angle bisectors, inscribed circle).
Sides → incenter; the angle bisectors put it equally far from each side.

widget.prompt: You need a point equidistant from all three SIDES of a triangular park (to place a sprinkler reaching each edge). Which center?

options.label: the incenter
options.feedback: Equidistant from the three SIDES is the incenter — center of the inscribed circle.

options.label: the circumcenter
options.feedback: The circumcenter is equidistant from the VERTICES, not the sides. For equal side distances, use the incenter.

options.label: the centroid
options.feedback: The centroid is the balance point, not equidistant from the sides. That's the incenter.

options.label: the orthocenter
options.feedback: The orthocenter has no equidistance property. Equal distance to the SIDES is the incenter.

steps.body: A quick memory hook by the LINES: **perpendicular bisectors → circumcenter**, **angle bisectors → incenter**, **medians → centroid**, **altitudes → orthocenter**. And by PROPERTY: two are equidistance centers (circum from vertices, in from sides), the centroid is the balance point, and the orthocenter is the odd one out with no special distance property.

widget.prompt: Match each center to its defining property.

pairErrors.feedback: Equidistant from SIDES is the incenter. The circumcenter is equidistant from VERTICES.
Equidistant from VERTICES is the circumcenter. The incenter is equidistant from SIDES.
The balance point is the centroid; equidistance from vertices is the circumcenter.

widget.missFeedback: Circum → vertices, in → sides, centroid → balance point.

explanationVariants: The balance point (center of mass) of a triangle is the centroid — where the medians meet.
To balance a triangular plate on a pin, use the centroid.

widget.prompt: To balance a thin triangular plate on the tip of a pencil, where does the pencil go?

options.label: the centroid
options.feedback: The centroid is the center of mass — the balance point where the medians meet.

options.label: the circumcenter
options.feedback: The circumcenter is about equal vertex distances, not balance — it can even lie outside. Use the centroid.

options.label: the incenter
options.feedback: The incenter is about equal side distances, not mass balance. The balance point is the centroid.

options.label: the orthocenter
options.feedback: The orthocenter is the altitudes' meeting, unrelated to balance. The centroid is the center of mass.

steps.body: Only two centers are guaranteed to stay INSIDE every triangle: the **centroid** and the **incenter**. The **circumcenter** and **orthocenter** slip outside when the triangle is obtuse. For a right triangle, the circumcenter lands exactly on the hypotenuse's midpoint — a handy special case.

widget.prompt: Which pair of centers always lies INSIDE the triangle, no matter its shape?

options.label: centroid and incenter
options.feedback: The balance point and the inscribed-circle center are always interior. Circumcenter and orthocenter can exit for obtuse triangles.

options.label: circumcenter and orthocenter
options.feedback: These two LEAVE the triangle when it's obtuse — they're the ones that can be outside, not always inside.

options.label: circumcenter and incenter
options.feedback: The incenter is always inside, but the CIRCUMcenter can fall outside an obtuse triangle. The always-inside pair is centroid and incenter.

options.label: centroid and orthocenter
options.feedback: The centroid is always inside, but the ORTHOcenter can fall outside. Pair the centroid with the incenter.

hints: A circle must pass THROUGH all three vertices — which center is its middle?
Passing through the vertices means equidistant from them.
explanationVariants: A circle through all three vertices is the circumscribed circle, centered at the circumcenter — the perpendicular-bisector meeting point equidistant from the vertices.

widget.prompt: You must draw the unique circle that passes through all three vertices of a triangle. Its center is the…

options.label: circumcenter
options.feedback: A circle through all three vertices is the circumscribed circle, centered at the circumcenter.

options.label: incenter
options.feedback: The incenter centers the circle touching the SIDES from inside, not one through the vertices. Use the circumcenter.

options.label: centroid
options.feedback: The centroid is the balance point, not equidistant from the vertices — so no single circle through them centers there. It's the circumcenter.

options.label: orthocenter
options.feedback: The orthocenter has no equidistance to the vertices. The circle through all three is centered at the circumcenter.

takeaways: Lines: perp bisectors→circumcenter, angle bisectors→incenter, medians→centroid, altitudes→orthocenter.
Properties: circum=equidistant from vertices, in=equidistant from sides, centroid=balance point.
Always inside: centroid and incenter; circumcenter and orthocenter can fall outside (obtuse).
steps.teaser: Next chapter: triangle inequalities — the hinge theorem and which side lengths can even form a triangle.
